Mr. Chairman, may I have the privilege of addressing you for a few moments in connection with the matter of grants to'Indian schools ? My right hon. friend the First Minister had the goodness to refer to me yesterday as an authority upon educational matters in connection with the young Indians. My information is perhaps obtained from sources that are as reliable as any that can be furnished, and I desire to submit a few observations in connection with the grants to Indian schools from the experience I have had in meeting the Six Nation Indians particularly for many years past. I may say that the Mohawk institution, that figures, I think, the fourth in the list of grants, is an institution with which I have had a good deal of familiarity and it is in reference to that particularly that I wish to speak. I may say that the grants that have been made from time to time to that institution have, I believe, for the most part, been very well expended. If I were sure that all the grants to all the Indian schools were of the same nature as that I should have no hesitation whatever in saying that it was well expended money. The question was asked, and my right hon. friend referred to me yesterday, in reference to what the effect was upon the rising generation of Indians. I may say that the effect has been for the most part very good indeed. It is perhaps not generally known that the county of Brant contains the largest reservation that exists in North America, that is in point of population, the population being upwards of 4,000. Contact with civilization has not acted as was generally expected it would in the destruction of the race. The race is actually upon the increase. I know from last year's report that it has increased some 63 in numbers. This fact then leads to an observation as to what is the ultimate destiny of our Indian race so far as the Six Nation Indians are concerned. I believe their destiny is not extinction but absorption, that they will ultimately be absorbed into the peoples of this country and become consolidated as a Canadian race. The white blood has now been

so infused into the race that there are comparatively few of pure blood there. This may appear to be surprising, but it is nevertheless the fact and we have to face the facts as they are. The race is likely to be absorbed among the population of Canada. Within probably three or five generations this change at the rate at which it is going on now, will have been completed. The question has been raised :	Is the money being
well expended which is devoted to the education of Indians ? I think I may say it has been well expended at the Mohawk institution. The grant that is made at present is some $60 per head for 91 pupils, although I see that they did not obtain last year the total of that grant for reasons that I cannot explain. They obtained from $4,700 to $4,900. I find that it is stated as $4,700 in one report and $4,900 in another, whereas they were entitled to some $5,400. This grant has been made for perhaps ten years or in the neighbourhood of ten years. It was first made when Mr. Dewdney was in charge of the department, and I think I had the honour of seeing him in connection with the grant at that time. It has been continued ever since and young Indians have been turned out from that institution who are filling many honourable positions iii the land. Residents of the city of Toronto well know that one of the most distinguished residents of Toronto was a former resident of the Six Nation reserve. He has obtained a salary which is not less than that of the First Minister sitting in this House and is at the head of one of the greatest financial institutions of this country. He is a former pupil of this- institution.
I would refer also to the fact that in the days of Sir John Macdonald, it was his custom to occasionally introduce into the Department of the Interior and the Indian service, graduates of note from the Six Nation reserve and there is one young lady still in the department. I would suggest to my right hon. friend that it would be wise to continue that custom introduced in the time of Sir John Macdonald. It furnishes an incentive to the young men of the Six Nations to make great efforts and I think that it is one of the object lessons that should be set before them. These are positions that they can fill and I think they are entitled to feel there are positions that they can occupy in this country. It should be remembered in discussing this question that the grants that are given to the Six Nations are largely taken out of their own moneys, that they are not a charge upon the country. These grants are derived largely from their own interest money and the Six Nation Indians are not a charge upon the people of the country. I know not whether they are considered constituents of my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) or of myself, but they are residents of the county of Brant, they are upwards of 4.000 in number and in the year 1887 my hon.

friend the Minister of Customs and myself had the honour of polling the first Indian vote ever polled for a white man in North America. This vote was fairly evenly divided. I think the disfranchising of the Indians was a step in the wrong direction, inasmuch as I believe the Indians of the Six Nations are advanced by conferring upon them the responsibilities of citizenship. They were enfranchised in 1885, I think, by Sir John Macdonald, and up to the year 1896 or 1897 they had the privilege of voting in Dominion elections. That has been discontinued owing to the provincial lists becoming operative and they are not qualified to vote in provincial matters. I believe the advantage of voting to the race was considerable.
I believe that right should be again conferred, although I am not in a position td ask for that to-day. I say that our ideal should be the absorption of these tribes by the people of the country. With that en.l in view, I think I may well say that they will become a credit to this country and that the money we are expending on the n is well expended. Probably no nation on the face of the earth has advanced more rapidly than the Six Nations of Brant county have done during the last century and a half. It is only a century and a half since they were a barbarous race; to-day many of them occupy well tilled farms and are in comfortable circumstances, and many ol them are capable of discharging duties in high stations. That is a fact to which I can vouch from my own observation. We have had no less than eight of these Indians in our own domestic service in fifteen years, and they have all acquitted themselves satisfactorily. If my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will inquire in the department, he will find that there is a young Indian lady there who for the past fifteen years has acquitted herself creditably and is to-day drawing a considerable salary .for efficient work. That is only a sample of what can be done and is being done through the instruction which is being obtained in the Mohawk institution.
I may say that the training given at that institution Is technical and manual ns well as educational, and this, I think, should be the basis of all instruction to the Indians; that is, they should be taught to work. We know that in former days, even in any earlier days, the redman's burden was carried by the Indian woman. To-day that condition has disappeared. This shows the advance of civilization among them. The only way to assist the Indians to advance to first-class civilization is to teach them to work.
The Iroquois, or Six Nations, are probably tbe most advanced tribe on tbe North American continent to-day, and their advancement is largely due to the work of the industrial school near the confines of the city of Brantford. That institution is maintained largely by the New England Com-

pany, of London, England, a charitable institution, and not the government, nor is it aided largely by public moneys. During this past year the Rt. Hon. the Earl of Stamford, a commissioner o-f the company, visited that institution, and also invests gated the schools on the Six Nations reserve. He went to Lytton, in British Columbia, also where the company has established an institution. As I said, these schools are almost entirely maintained ns charities by the New England Company, and the government grant is a small proportion of the money expended on them. That being the case, I trust that when a further grant is asked, as I think it will bo at an early day, for the purpose of furnishing fire protection for the new institution, my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier) will view that application favourably, and that the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) will join with me in (pressing the necessity of a grant towards this crying need of this institution. You will remember that it was burned down eighteen months ago. The buildings, which were totally destroyed, have been replaced with the insurance money, but fire protection is still required. Water mains are being laid by the city of Brantford into the country, and it is expected that it will cost $8,000 to provide the fire protection. The New England Company have applied to the department for $3,000 towards this expense, and I would be very glad if my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid -Laurier) could see his way to granting that request. The -lives of the children would be in danger in the event of a fire under present conditions. I trust that when this matter comes up for consideration it will not be viewed from any party standpoint, as the remarks I am making are not made in any factious spirit or with a desire to unduly criticise; my desire is to point out the -fact that the institution is worthy of the grant it is now getting, -and should also receive a further grant of $3,000 towards fire protection. That grant would be appreciated not only by the Mohawk Institute but also by the Six Nations, who are a large part, probably 10 per cent, of the population of Brant.
The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) yesterday referred to pagan rites on this reserve. I am free to admit that they are still practised, but to a very small extent. My hon. friend says he saw them when he was there. I admit that the practice still exists, but not 10 per cent of the Six Nations or Iroquois are to-day pagans; I think less than 300 out of 4,000. It is true that the white dog is occasionally sacrificed and that the green corn dance takes place, but the occurrence of these rites is duo to the white man rather than the Indian. The Indians cater for the audience that applies for the ancient rites, and if our intelligent white men would cease to demand this kind of entertainment these rites
would cease. I am not blaming the Canadians particularly, as I believe that the British visitors are more to blame than the Canadians. They pass the Church of England, the Presbyterian Church, the Methodist Church and the Roman Catholic Church and -drive to -the long house, in order that they may see these rites performed, as they are something they -have never seen before. That causes the -Six Nations to continue the rites although they have long ceased to have any meaning. Of the 4,000 Indians in the county, a large majority are professing Christianity. I trust that when my hon. -friend visits the reserve he will visit some of the other schools and churches ; there he will not see war paint, but men seated and in their right minds, worshipping God in the -same way as we all worship Him. The Indians are, of course, largely of the Church of England, and come under the heading, as I do myself, of miserable sinners. The Mohawk chu-rch is attended by the pupils of the Mohawk institute, 125 or 130 in number, and there is also a white congregation of six or eight, of which I am generally one when I am at home. I hear them every Sabbath, and I may say for the benefit of gentlemen on both sides of tlie House, that whenever they are in Brantford, if they attend service at this church, they will hear a service of which they may be.proud, and will feel satisfied that the little grant made by the government of Canada towards the institution and the Mohawk church is well expended. I may say as a matter of information that the King of England during the past year has granted to the Mohawk church the privilege of being known as His Majesty's Chapel of the Mohawks. That is a privilege which the Mohawks enjoyed in the old days in the United States, and they were promised when they came into the Grand River valley that they would have the -same privilege there, but it was on-ly in the past year, through the Earl of Stamford and the late Governor General, Lord Minto, that application was made to the King for this privilege, which he has been graciously pleased to grant. This house of God, in which these pupils of the Mohawk Institute worship, is maintained by the New England Company, and the incumbent of the church is also the superintendent of the school. I think that the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) will agree with me that the affairs of that institution, under the management of the New England Company 

because, as I have said, it is not a government institution-have been well and faithfully administered for upwards of seventy-five years. The church and institute have been a great boon for the Six Nations, and it is through their influence that the Six Nations, although they were first in war in the old days, are to-day first of the native Indian tribes in the arts of civilization and peace. That is the reputation which this

nation to-day enjoys, and I trust that this item, which refers to the grant to the Mohawk Institute will be increased. I thank the hon. gentleman for the opportunity which he has given me of making these few remarks in connection with an institution in which I take a deep interest.

Are the troubles at Oka between the Indians and the seminary now over?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry to say that the trouble is not over, but I am not without hope that it may be got over. We have lately had correspondence upon this subject, and there has been an agreement, not completed, but in the way of completion, to have the rights which are claimed by the Indians and disputed by the seminary, as to the land in question, referred to the Privy Council. Counsel have been empjoyed on both sides, in order to have the question submitted in the proper way for a judicial* decision. I may say, speaking not officially, but on behalf of the department, that the government have agreed to this, and intend to ask for an appropriation from parliament to cover the expenses of the Indians.

What lips become of the arrangements which were made between the government of Canada and the Indians of Oka, in 1882, I believe, by which the Indians were to surrender their rights on condition of the seminary buying a piece of land for them in the township of Gibson in Ontario ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: A piece of land was bought in the township of Gibson, on the Georgian bay, but there was never any official agreement between the Indians and the seminary in regard to it. A good many Indians left the reserve at Oka and went to Gibson to settle, but I understand that the greater part of them came back to Oka again. The Indians are under the impression that they have an absolute title to the land, that the grant made by the King of France to the seminary did not deprive them of any of their rights. This is disputed by the seminary, and until we can have a judicial determination of the question, it is impossible to expect that there will be peace in the locality. Every one of the Indians is absolutely convinced that the seminary are trespassers, and that they are the true owners of the. soil. We have asked them to agree to submit the matter to the judicial decision of the Privy Council. and I understand that they are willing to do so. The seminary are also ready to have the question of their title submitted to the courts.

Was not the sum of $16,000 paid to purchase the property which Mr. COCKSHUTT.
was to be substituted for the Oka reserve? What is to become of that money?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The seminary agreed to pay and did pay $16,000 for the township of Gibson; but two years ago the money was returned to the seminary except the part which is actually held by Indians.
How is it that we are paying salaries to these Oka Indian chiefs? I do not see any such payments made to the chiefs of other reserves.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Most of the bands have funds of their own; but the Oka Indians have no money of their own, and therefore we pay $50 to the chief of the band at Gibson, also $50 to two other chiefs.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Last year, I believe, there was a general increase.

I find in the Auditor General's Report that bonuses were paid to the permanent messengers ranging from $50 to $100 for the session of 1903. I am not making any objection to that, because all these were good men, and perhaps deserving of the recognition that was given to them. But I think the practice is a vicious one, and I hope His Honour the Speaker will not continue it. If it is desirable to increase the salaries of the messengers, it should be increased permanently, I think. But what I am desirous of ascertaining is whether the $50 bonus which was given to the permanent messengers for the session of 1903, was made a permanent addition to their salaries, and whether they had reached the maximum by having that addition made to their salaries earlier than they otherwise would have done.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The clerk informs me that the bonus was given owing to the length of the session, and was not to be a permanent increase.

That is not a very satisfactory explanation, because these gentlemen were employed for the whole year. I am not finding any fault with granting bonuses to them, but they are employed for the whole year. It matters little what the length of the session may be, they have to be here the whole year round. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

He always had to do that.

Do we understand then that what formerly was done by a permanent messenger detailed for that service while the House was in session, which messenger had his own duties during the remainder of the year to perform, is now done by another official, that now we have been advanced to this other stage that the Speaker has a full fledged steward of his own who comes when the Speaker comes, who goes when the Speaker goes, and who has no duties during any other part of the year ? I have not been able to find out exactly from what Mr. Speaker has said as to whether that is the condition of things or whether this steward comes back to his work when the Speaker leaves at the adjournment of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

I know this was an arrangement made by the late Speaker, and not by the present one, but at the same time we ought to have an answer.

I see in the Auditor General's Rejjort, O-20, a number of items that have a very familiar appearance. Such items as books and maps for instance, 95 Canadian Parliamentary Guides, $70 ; Canadian Politics, $5.40 ; Canadian Annual, $3.80; Canadian Annual Review, $46.35 ; New Dictionary of Larousse, $43 ; Political Appointments to Parliament and the Judical Bench of Canada, $60, and so on. Who supervises these purchases and who is responsible for seeing that they remain the property of the government ? Then there are considerable purchases of furniture every year. It is most extraordinary what a quantity has to be purchased each year, and one wonders what becomes of all the things purchased. There are purchases of desks and tables and all sorts of things from Bryson, Graham & Co., amounting to $999.13. Also from J. O. Leblanc for desks and lounges and chairs amounting to $421,50. Also from Harris, Campbell & Boyden Furniture Company, desks and tables aild chairs to the extent of $157.75. I need not take up the time of the committee in going through the list, but I remember well when years ago pages of that kind were read in the House. Who is in charge when the House rises and the Speaker goes away, and who is responsible that that furniture is not taken away from the building ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

As regards the desks, I have been Speaker only a few days and in that time have received quite a number of requisitions from gentlemen on both sides to be furnished with desks. No doubt my predecessors have had similar experience. Of course, as in a private house, furniture gets used up and has to be replaced from time to time. In this respect we are much less fortunate than some of the older provinces, who seem to have all the good things of this life. Walking along one of the upper corridors we find a room whose door is marked ' N.B. Members.' As far as I can learn, that means N.B. Grit members. I would advise Mr. Speaker to have the word ' Grit ' painted before ' N.B.' There is a room there, but if a Tory puts his head in, he is apt to be requested to get out.

I can say, on the authority of a former Speaker of this House, that there is no room in this House which any member is not free to enter. And I can remember a case where this former Speaker said that if any person put a lock on any room in the House and any member wished to enter that room, he would send his locksmith to open it.

Now that this matter is up, I certainly think it should be made clear that if there are to be rooms for any* there must be rooms for all. It should all be done on some systematic basis, and fair-play should be shown. I trust that Mr. Speaker will see to it that the leader of the Conservative opposition in this House is given an additional room adjoining his own, where his secretary can work.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
This discussion should show us that it is about,, time for the House to' consider how business is to be done. There is, no doubt, just ground for complaint on the part of members on both sides. Many of us have a large correspondence to attend to, and the majority must attend to that correspondence in their places in this chamber or somewhere else, no special accommodation being afforded. We should provide in some way proper accommodations for the members of the House. I understand that in the United States a member of Congress is given an allowance for a secretary and is also given a room in which to do his workj In this House, under the previous administration, I am informed, the members of the Liberal opposition had to do their work in the corridors of the House. Looking over the list of rooms that has been posted in>
this House, I find that our friends of fijie opposition have no great reason to complain in comparison with the members on this side. If they complain, I would like them to refer to the distribution of rooms of about ten years ago, and they will see what insignificant accommodation was given to the opposition of that time. I find that at present our friends of the opposition have the following rooms, outside of the rooms provided for the leader and the whips :-Room No. C, Conservative headquarters ; No. 34, Conservative members ; No. 36, Ontario Conservative members ; No. 37, Conservative ex-ministers; No. 56, Conservative members from Ontario ; No. 72, Conservative members-Messrs. White and Foster. Here we have six rooms in all. On the Liberal side we find that, apart from the rooms occupied by some of the ministers, including the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, there are the following:-Room No. 16, Liberal headquarters ; No. 48, Northwest Territories members ; No. 58, Liberal members from Ontario ; No. 49. Chairman of the Printing Committee and members from Ontario ; No. 67, Liberal members from New Brunswick ; No. 68, Liberal) members from Nova Scotia ; No. 69, Chairman of the Debates Committee and some Liberal members ; No. 71, liberal members of the province of Quebec-eight rooms in all. So that the opposition, with a membership of 76, have six rooms, while the government side, with a membership of 138, or nearly double, have only eight rooms. I think the comparison does not give our friends on the other side anything to complain of. But, outside of the comparison, all the members have something to complain of in the accommodation afforded. I presume that many members have an average mail of from twenty-five to thirty-five letters a day. Where are we to answer these letters ? If we dictate to a stenographer, where is the work to be done ? As you walk about, you see members even sitting in the corridors dictating their correspondence. Go into the Railway Committee

Room, and you find stenographers here and there writing at the dictation of members. This is not in accordance with the dignity of the House or with the work we have to do. We do not come here to play, but each of us bears a certain responsibility and has important work to do. Members on the government side of the House may have a great many questions of patronage arising in their counties, involving a large correspondence, for the carrying on of which there it now no accommodation. This discussion will have done good if it arouses the government and the House to the necessity of providing better accommodation for the members in the immediate future.
Perhaps Mr. Speaker will provide a few desks for Tories in that room he spoke of. If he does, I will take my chances on getting into the room.

The room referred to by Mr. Speaker as affording accommodation for Conservative members from the maritime provinces is sometimes occupied by the sittings of the Committee on Agriculture. Besides, if it is to be lumbered up with many more desks, it will not be possible to do work there any better than at our desks in this chamber. It will be in the interest of the House and of the country to provide better accommodation, for members would then have opportunities for research and study, and could better fit themselves for the discussion of public questions. At least rooms should be provided for the members on either side from the different provinces. New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and other provinces have been named. I will put in a word on behalf of the members from Prince Edward Island. Witli the work of the country growing every year, and, as the hon. member from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) says, with members receiving an average of from twenty-five to thirty letters a day, it is impossible to do the work unless members are given better accommodation. Outside of the discussion whether the rooms should be given to Liberals or Conservatives, I think it would be well for the government to take into consideration the matter of providing better accommodation for members.

There is another matter to which I wish to draw the attention of the Speaker and the House. At the present moment I am informed the full lights are turned on, and we have practically' only' twilight in this chamber. A few years ago we had a very good light, and it was changed for some purpose or other, and since then.it has been very inadequate. I would respectfully suggest that the candle power should be at least doubled in this chamber. Getting old as some of us are, we find it is absolutely necessary to have the chamber better lighted. I think the old apparatus is still here, and why not combine that with the present system?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This being the first session of a new parliament and a new Speaker, I would now venture to make the suggestion that I made when the Conservative party were in power, and which I think would have been acted on had they remained in power another session, that is, to provide more accommodation for the members of both sides, to which I think they are justly entitled. The suggestion I made then, and that I make now, is that we provide accommodation outside the House of Commons for the Speaker, the sergeant-at-arms and the chief messenger. I think the House of Commons should be reserved altogether for the use of members. I do not think it would be any more difficult for the Speaker, the sergeant-at-arms and the chief messenger to go to their lodgings at night than it is for the Prime- Minister, the other members of the government and the House of Commons. We all have to make our way home. I do not see the necessity for any of these gentlemen being housed in this building. The restaurant people also-they all have too much accommodation taken away from the members. These gentlemen should have quarters, they should have rooms here; but there is no necessity' for the larger part of the House of Commons being taken up by the Speaker, the deputy speaker, the sergeant-at-arms and the chief messenger. These gentlemen should be provided with respectable quarters outside. I know the present Speaker and the former Speakers would prefer living in respectable quarters outside. In this way accommodation could be provided so that every man, or groups of a few members, could have rooms where they could do their private correspondence without being obliged to do it at their desks, as most of us have to do. I make this suggestion to the Speaker and to the Prime Minister, that arrangements be made immediately for removing all the families now living in the House of Commons and putting them in permanent quarters outside, allotting the rooms vacated proportionately between the members supporting the government and those supporting the opposition.	,

In the constituency I come from we are in the habit of considering the rights of the ladies. I have noticed that there is no general waiting-room in this House for the convenience of ladies. I think there ought to be such a room for ladies who come here from a distance, no matter what may be their political leanings, a room with all the proper conveniences which they would expect to find in connection therewith.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I can inform the gallant member who has just spoken (Mr. Miller) that now, for the first time in any session, there has been a nicely furnished cloak room provided upstairs for ladies, and a couple of attendants are there to see that

tlieir wants are provided for. That is a move in the right direction. The whole matter has been very fully discussed, and I can assure the House that I will bring it promptly to the attention of the government, and perhaps make some future reference to it.

Before we pass from this subject I would like to say a word more with reference to the sessional writers. I see by the Auditor General's Report that whilst the general sessional writers are paid $4 a day, Mr. P! A. Stewart and Mr. Tache are paid $600 each for the session. Has there been anj7 increase in the salaries of these gentlemen since this report was published? They have enjoyed that salary for a long series of years, and were getting $600 a year when the sessional writers were only getting $3 a day. I would like to know whether any increases have been made in the salaries of these gentlemen, because we have the curious anomaly here of the two chief sessional writers getting $600 a year each, and their subordinates getting a larger sum during the session of 1904. That should not continue. These chief sessional writers ought at least to get a larger pay than the ordinary sessional writers.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There has been no permanent increase in the salaries for the last two sessions. The sessions of 1903 and 1904 were very long, and an extra allowance was made on that score of $300 each.

Would it not be better that a permanent addition be made to the salaries of these gentlemen than that they should be dependent upon the will of the Speaker for an increase? They are both good men, at least they were in former times. I suppose Mr. Stewart must be pretty well advanced in years, but they both discharge their duties efficiently. Yet it seems anomalous that, according to the Auditor General's Report, they are receiving a less sum than their subordinates. It seems to me that these two gentlemen, instead of being dependent upon getting a bonus whenever it pleases the Speaker or the Committee on Internal Economy to give them a bonus, should have a permanent addition to their salaries.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The suggestion is worthy of consideration, and will be considered.

With reference to the books, as I understand, Mr. Speaker, these books which were purchased under the direction of the clerk go towards filling out the clerk's personal library, I mean his official library. _

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, and the translators' library. Some are transferred to the library.

I notice in some cases there are a number ot copies of the same book, as for instance of the Canadian An-Mr. SPEAKER.
nual Review, a very good book, and I dare say it is well used. There are a dozen copies of that document.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: These are distributed to the leading officials of the House as being useful to them in their work.

I agree with the opinion of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan), except that I do not think we have as much accommodation as he says. Only a few' of us have a room to work in. We are eleven members of the opposition from Quebec, and not one of us has a room to himself. The whole opposition has room No. 6, and those who were there in the old time know how inadequate is that room for seventy-five members. I think that this practice of separating the members in that way does more harm than good. Why not move them together more ? Instead of having one room for the Liberal members and another for the Conservative, why not let all the members from New7 Brunswick, say, have one room, and the same with the members from Quebec, and with every other province ? There is no reason why the members on both sides of the House should not be perfectly friendly and near one another while attending to their private correspondence. I am afraid it will lengthen the session if we do not get a room. We have to stay here. I am very glad to be able to state publicly w'hat the conditions are so that the people w7ho have correspondence with us will know why it is that they sometimes do not get answers. I cannot write letters here. 1 can go to No. 6, but I cannot do any work there because there are so many gentlemen speaking in the room. I cannot be here five minutes until gentlemen come and engage in conversation so that it is impossible to do any work here. We should have some quarters where w7e could work. I ask the right hon. Prime Minister how7 a member can prepare any serious work in a place like this. It is impossible to do it. The consequence is that if we are not well prepared with our work we may delay the House, because our speeches may be longer than they would be if we had an opportunity of preparing them more thoroughly.
Customs-salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in the various provinces and in the Northwest Territories, including pay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $1,214,865.
There was a question raised some time ago in Montreal in regard to the appointment of a deputy collector. I have not yet heard whether the question has been settled or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No, there has not been any deputy collector appointed.
Was there a demand or a suggestion to that effect ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Well, I have heard it suggested, but 1 would uot call it a demaud. There has been no deputy collector since Mr. O'Hara died. The department has not felt the necessity of it. We have no deputy anywhere.

Did my hon. friend get a demand from the trade of Montreal to the effect that Mr. White, the collector, had not time to answer all the questions which were put to him in the custom house there as the business of the port is very extensive ? A petition was presented by the trade of Montreal to that effect. I understand it was supported by the present collector and that it contained the statemenlt that it would be in the interest of the trade at that port to have a deputy collector appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Perhaps there has been a petition. If there has been it has been lately. It has been running in my mind that I had seen something in the papers about it, but there has been no action.
There has been no decision ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No.
Will the hon. minister take this item up by the different provinces and tell us what are the increases in each-or by ports, whichever he chooses ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: We have not the estimate in that way.

In what way has the hon. minister the estimate ? Everything is lumped here. You have simply a line or two and a million and a quarter of dollars at the end of it. What is the system of explanation there ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Largely comparing one year with another. The only increase asked for this year is for the salaries and contingencies of the various ports. We are asking $20,000 more.
Mr. POSTER, Will the hon. minister take it up by ports ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No.
How then ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: In a general way. If the hon. gentleman wants to know what has been expended last year in the different provinces by way of increase, I can give him that, and as it has been done in one year the presumption is that you may require to have something done in that way during the coming year, either in the way of new appointments which have been found necessary or in the way of increases that may have been given in the department.

Does the hon. minister say that he is not able to take it up by ports ? That seems to be the only way in which it
can be fairly followed. Which province will the hon. minister take up first ? I suppose as Ontario occupies a very prominent position in the eyes of the world the hon. minister might take up Ontario first.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Last year we asked for an additional vote of $35,000.
For Ontario ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: No, for the whole Dominion. There was absorbed of that by increases $22,000 in round numbers. I have a list of how they were distributed if the bon. gentleman wants it. Does he want the individual names or does he want the bulk sums ?
That is for the increased expenses of last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes, for the increases in salaries last year. I can give it to him by provinces if he desires it with all the names.
I suppose that is the way we will have to get at it.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: In that way or will the hon. gentleman take it in bulk at so much ?	_
Well, it is much easier for the hon. gentleman if we take it in the bulk, but I am afraid we would not get much information.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
If I read the names would the hon. gentleman know the officers anyway, or would it assist him in any way?
Mr. POSTER, I have here the towns and Ports and officers and everything in connection with each port. The only way you can follow it is to take them as they appear in the Auditor General's Report.
Mr. PATER-SON. I will give merely the bulk sums to the hon. gentleman and then if it will help him, I will give him the names of the officers at the differents ports. In the province of Ontario we increased the salaries of 72 officers.
That is last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Out of the amount voted last year-the increase being $5,060. In Quebec we increased the salaries of 77 officers, the total increase being $5,076. In New Brunswick seven officers have been increased, making $500 in all. In Nova Scotia 37 officers had an increase.
New Brunswick seven, and Nova Scotia thirty-seven, and yet somebody wonders why Nova Scotia went solid.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: New Brunswick went pretty nearly that way too.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The thirty-seven amounted to $3,210, in Manitoba there were



twenty-two increases totalling $3,050, and in British Columbia forty-nine increases amounting to $5,180. In Prince Edward Island we had eight increases coming to $450, in the Northwest Territories we have six increases amounting to $600. That it to say we were able last year to increase the salaries in all of 278 officers at a cost of $22.-186. We are asking for $20,000 extra this year.
You had an unexpended vote last year of $11,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Yes, there was that amount unexpended. So this year we are only asking $22,000 out of which we will make our increases, although of course I may have to ask for a supplementary vote as we can judge better towards the end of the session.
Mr. FOSTER On what basis are these increases made? There are such things as regular increases and special increases.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: In the outside service .there is no regular increase.
But there is the custom.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The custom is efficiency and the work performed. Last year we gave increases chiefly to the men who were getting small salaries of $500 and $600. We were not able to do so much for the higher classes of officers some of whom of course deserved it, and in some cases these increases were given.
Mr! FOSTER. How does the minister get ids information as to the officei's to whom increases should be given ? On the report of what officers ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The collectors and the inspectors. Of course we can see for ourselves where a salary is only $500 or $600, and the commissioner has often reported to me verbally that in his view no officer should be paid less than $600. It has been urged upon us that the cost of living has increased lately and we now have most of our officers up to the $600 mark.

I do not suppose the minister, for instance in Ottawa, takes his list of officers and finding a man who last year was getting $450 would say to his secretary,
* now increase that man to $500 ' because he might be increasing a man who is altogether inefficient, and even if a man has a low salary if he is inefficient in his work he is scarcely deserving of an increase. There must be some method by which information comes to the head of the department here, the minister, on which he makes his decision as to the increase so as to be able to know that undeserving men do not get increases. Of course in the statistical branch the minister would have the information here. He knows when the officer is appointed and how many years he has Mr. PATERSON.
been in the service. How does the minister acquire information as to outside officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: We confer with the collectors and inspectors with respect to that. I might say to the hon. gentleman that we are communicated with by the officers themselves, and we make inquiries in reference to them and ascertain from our inspectors as to the services they are rendering, and upon that information we make up our minds whether we should grant the increase.
Is that all the information my hon. friend has, is that the only system?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: That is the only system.
My hon. friend never receives letters or representations?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Oh, yes.
These count?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes, but we cannot trust to these, you know ; we must have the official information.

Take for instance Halifax. Is there a report required by the minister's department here as to the general condition and efficiency of the work in the port of Halifax, say in the customs house? Are these things reported on to Ottawa where the salaries are ultimately decided.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes, there is such a system.
From all ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes, we have in Nova Scotia, Mr. Bremner and Mr. McDonnell-Mr. Hill was witii us for thirty-five or forty years but he has passed away, and Mr. McDonnell was appointed in his place. We have also had for many years Mr. Bremner. They visit all the ports and we expect a report from every port in the Dominion at least once a year. I think we have it oftener in some cases. We have in Ontario now a chief inspector and three officers.
I would ask the Minister of Customs what salary the customs collector at Coatswortli, in my own constituency of West Kent, receives and what the returns for the last fiscal year for that port were ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
What is the name of the port ?
. Mr. CLEMENTS. I do not know. It is a few miles from Romney.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Thomas Robinson is the collector, and he receives $400.
What are the revenue returns from that office ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs

speechtext: While I think a port is necessary in that district, I think it is in the wrong place. I think the town of Wheatley, about five miles from there, is the proper place. I would ask the hon. minister to take that into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I shall be very glad to inquire as to that. I judge, from the small amount of revenue returned that it must be largely a preventive station. Does the hon. gentleman say that Wheatley would be a better point to prevent smuggling than where the office is now V
Yes.
What increases of salaries were made at the Galt customs house ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The salary of Mr. Denis, the preventive officer, was advanced from $600 to $650. The collector has asked for an increase, but it was not given last year. It is under consideration.

I represent a large district, the district of Muskoka, in which there is no custom house at all, and we find it very inconvenient in getting goods in. I am sure that the revenue of that district is much larger than that of many others which have custom houses.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: We have had strong representations from portions of Muskoka on that subject, among others from Brace-bridge, a large and thriving place. During the summer months, when there is a good deal of traffic, we have an office at Graven-hurst. We have had applications for new offices from thirty or forty places, but it is difficult to accommodate them all. The opening of every new port means an additional expenditure. Then, while we are very anxious to oblige the business community as far as we can, we are not able to secure the same judgment with reference to values and as to whether invoices are correct, at many of these points that we can at larger points, where we can afford to pay larger salaries and have men especially delegated for the work. In the United States there are only a few very large ports. I believe it is a fact that for their 80,000,000 people, they have not as many ports as we have in Canada-not relatively, but absolutely. But the people of Canada have been accustomed to having conveniences nearer home. I can well understand what the hon. gentleman says as to the strong claims of the district he represents; but the department feel that the fewer ports we can have, with due convenience to the people, the greater uniformity in values we can secure.
Have you any system for opening "new offices, with reference to size or population ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I do not think there is any pressing demand for increases there. 1 think we are pretty well manned there.
Mr. BARKER, I think so, too ; but there will be a great deal of disappointment if some appointments are not made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Would it be a disappointment to the sitting members ?
No. but to some very strong supporters of the right hon. gentleman who expect offices.
In the United .States, where there is a small number of ports comparatively, taking into account its population, how do they overcome what seem to be great difficulties to us ?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I suppose the business is done through brokers, with power of attorney.
That system is also in vogue here.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Yes. in the larger cities, but we are under no responsibility to the brokers.
I see there are very large increases in Nova Scotia compared with New Brunswick. How does my hon. friend account for that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
In New Brunswick the officers were better paid, and in raising the pay in Nova Scotia we are bringing the officers there on a footing more nearly equal to those of New Brunswick.
Some resolutions reported.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.
Can the Prime Minister give us any information as to the probable time when the Bill for the establishment of the Northwest province, or provinces, will be ready ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot give any definite information to-day.
I suppose it will be as soon as possible ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes ; I am very anxious to do so. I suppose that ilex' week we shall commence a more regular

course of business than we have had up to this time. I should think that the bill referred to could be introduced probably during the second week in February.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 6 p.ru.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Monday, January 30, 1905.
